q: An Event Grid subscription uses the default retry policy, and the webhook endpoint is down. How long and how many times does Event Grid try to deliver an event?
o: 24 hours or 30 attempts, whichever comes first
7 days or 100 attempts, whichever comes first
Exactly 3 attempts within the first minute
Until the endpoint recovers, with no time limit
e: By default Event Grid retries delivery for 24 hours (1,440 minutes) or 30 times, whichever limit is reached first, using an exponential backoff schedule. After that the event is dead-lettered if a dead-letter location is configured, otherwise it is dropped.

q: Events older than 2 hours are useless to your handler. How should you configure the event subscription?
o: Set the retry policy's event time-to-live to 120 minutes
Set maxDeliveryAttempts to 120
Configure a custom retry schedule of every 2 hours
Set the subscription expiration time to 2 hours from now
e: The retry policy has two settings: maximum delivery attempts (1 to 30) and event time-to-live (1 to 1,440 minutes). Setting the TTL to 120 minutes stops retries after 2 hours. The retry schedule itself can't be configured, and the subscription expiration deletes the whole subscription at a given time.

q: You want events that Event Grid couldn't deliver to be kept for later analysis instead of being dropped. What should you configure?
o: A dead-letter destination: a blob container set on the event subscription
A Service Bus dead-letter queue that is attached to the custom topic
A longer event retention period configured on the custom topic itself
A second event subscription that points to the same webhook endpoint
e: Event Grid dead-lettering writes undeliverable events to a blob container in a storage account that you specify on the event subscription (for example with --deadletter-endpoint). Without it, events are dropped when retries end. Service Bus DLQs belong to Service Bus, topics have no such TTL setting, and a second subscription to the same failing endpoint fails too.

q: Which values are valid when you customize an Event Grid subscription's retry policy?
o: Max delivery attempts 1–30 and event TTL 1–1,440 minutes
Max delivery attempts 1–100 and a custom backoff schedule
Event time-to-live of up to 7 days and unlimited attempts
A fixed retry interval, such as every 10 seconds, up to 1 day
e: Max delivery attempts must be an integer from 1 to 30, and event TTL must be from 1 to 1,440 minutes; the default for both is the maximum. You can't configure the retry schedule, which uses exponential backoff, and TTL can't exceed 24 hours.

q: An Azure Function subscribed to a Storage account's events should run only for blobs created under the container images whose names end with .jpg. Which filter settings should you use?
o: BlobCreated event type, subjectBeginsWith .../containers/images/blobs/, subjectEndsWith .jpg
An advanced filter on data.url with StringContains images, and no event type filter at all
No filter on the subscription; check the container and file extension inside the function
subjectEndsWith /containers/images/ and subjectBeginsWith .jpg, with the BlobCreated event type
e: Event type filters select BlobCreated events, and subject filters match the blob path prefix and suffix, as in Microsoft's subscription schema example. Filtering in the function still delivers and bills every event, a single contains check on the URL is less precise, and the last option reverses prefix and suffix.

q: You need to deliver only events whose data.color is blue, red, or green. Which kind of filter should you use?
o: An advanced filter: data.color StringIn [blue, red, green]
A subject filter with subjectBeginsWith set to blue, red, green
An event type filter that lists blue, red, and green as types
A dead-letter filter that drops the other colors after delivery
e: Advanced filters compare a key in the event, including fields inside data, against values using operators such as StringIn, NumberGreaterThan, or StringContains; StringIn matches any of the listed values. Subject and event type filters only inspect those specific fields, and there's no dead-letter filter.

q: An event subscription has two advanced filters: data.region StringIn [EU] and data.amount NumberGreaterThan 1000. Which events are delivered?
o: Only events that match both filters
Events that match either of the filters
Only the first filter is evaluated for each event
All events, because advanced filters are informational
e: When a subscription has several advanced filters, an event must satisfy all of them (logical AND). Within one filter, multiple values are combined with OR, so StringIn [EU, US] would match either value.

q: You create an Event Grid custom topic and publish events from your app. How must the request be authenticated?
o: An access key (aeg-sas-key), a SAS token, or Microsoft Entra ID
No authentication, because custom topics accept anonymous events
The storage account key of the subscriber that receives the events
A client certificate only, registered on the topic's Networking blade
e: Publishers authenticate to a custom topic with its access key, a SAS token generated from it, or a Microsoft Entra token for an identity with a publisher role. Topics aren't anonymous, subscriber storage keys aren't used for publishing, and client certificates aren't the documented mechanism.

q: When you create an Event Grid custom topic, which input schemas can you choose for the events you publish?
o: Event Grid, CloudEvents v1.0, or a custom mapped schema
Only CloudEvents v1.0, because it is the open standard
Only Avro, with a schema registered for each event type
Only the Service Bus message format with JSON bodies
e: The input schema of a custom topic is set when it is created: the Event Grid schema (the default), the CloudEvents v1.0 schema, or a custom event schema with input mappings to Event Grid fields. Avro and Service Bus formats aren't Event Grid input schemas.

q: Your existing system emits events with fields named eventName and eventSubject, and you can't change the publisher. How can you publish them to Event Grid?
o: Use a custom input schema that maps eventName and eventSubject to eventType and subject
Rename the fields in every subscriber so they read eventName and eventSubject instead
Use the CloudEvents schema, which accepts any field names that the publisher sends
Event Grid can't accept events that use other field names, so the publisher must change
e: Custom input schema mapping lets a topic map your fields to the Event Grid schema (id, eventTime, subject, eventType, dataVersion), with default values for subject, event type, and data version when they are missing. CloudEvents has its own required attributes, and subscribers can't fix publisher-side schema problems.

q: Which statement about CloudEvents in Azure Event Grid is correct?
o: Event Grid natively supports CloudEvents v1.0 JSON for system and custom events
CloudEvents is only supported for IoT Hub events, not for other system topics
CloudEvents always requires a custom input schema mapping on the topic
CloudEvents can only be delivered to Event Hubs, not to webhooks or functions
e: Event Grid natively supports CloudEvents v1.0 in JSON with the HTTP protocol binding, for system events such as Blob Storage and IoT Hub and for custom events. It is described as the preferred format because it's an open, extensible standard that improves interoperability. Event Grid also keeps its own proprietary schema.

q: You create an event subscription that targets your own HTTPS webhook using the Event Grid schema. Before any events are delivered, Event Grid sends a SubscriptionValidationEvent. What must your endpoint do?
o: Echo the validationCode in a validationResponse (or use the validationUrl)
Return HTTP 401 to prove that the endpoint is protected by authentication
Do nothing, because validation is optional for HTTPS webhook endpoints
Send a reply event to the custom topic that contains the subscription ID
e: To prevent abuse, Event Grid confirms that the endpoint wants the events through a validation handshake: the endpoint echoes the validationCode in a validationResponse, or someone browses to the validationUrl. Until validation succeeds, nothing is delivered. Returning 401 fails validation.

q: You subscribe a webhook with the CloudEvents v1.0 delivery schema. How does Event Grid confirm the endpoint?
o: The CloudEvents handshake: an OPTIONS request answered with WebHook-Allowed-Origin
A SubscriptionValidationEvent with a validationCode, as with the Event Grid schema
It requires the endpoint to be an Azure Function, which validates automatically
It skips validation entirely for CloudEvents, because the schema includes a source
e: When the CloudEvents schema is used for delivery, Event Grid uses the CloudEvents v1.0 abuse protection mechanism, an OPTIONS request that the endpoint must answer with the allowed origin header, in place of the Event Grid validation event. Validation is always required, and any HTTPS endpoint that implements it can be used.

q: Which requirement applies to a webhook endpoint that receives events pushed from Event Grid?
o: It must use HTTPS and handle webhook validation
It must be hosted in Azure in a supported service
It must accept FTP uploads for batched events
It must be in the same region as the Event Grid topic
e: Any public endpoint can be an event handler if it uses encryption in transit (HTTPS), can read the event format, and handles webhook validation. It doesn't have to be hosted in Azure or in the same region.

q: An Event Grid topic delivers events to a Service Bus queue. Security requires no keys or connection strings. How should delivery be authenticated?
o: Give the topic a managed identity with a Service Bus sender role, and deliver with it
Store the Service Bus connection string in the event subscription's delivery settings
Make the Service Bus namespace public and allow anonymous sends from Event Grid
Use the topic's access key on the Service Bus queue so both sides share one secret
e: Event Grid can deliver to Service Bus, Event Hubs, and Storage queues using its managed identity: enable a system- or user-assigned identity on the topic and add it to the right role on the destination. Connection strings are exactly what you wanted to avoid, Service Bus doesn't allow anonymous sends, and topic keys only authenticate publishers to Event Grid.

q: Which description best matches when to choose Azure Event Grid over Service Bus or Event Hubs?
o: Reacting to discrete events, such as a blob being created, with push delivery to many subscribers
Processing high-value business commands that need ordering, transactions, and dead-letter handling
Ingesting millions of telemetry records per second for stream analytics
Long-term storage of messages for months
e: Event Grid is an eventing service for discrete events that report state changes and pushes them to subscribers. Service Bus is a message broker for high-value commands with features like sessions, transactions, and DLQs, and Event Hubs is built for high-volume streaming telemetry. None of them is long-term message storage.

q: Your event handler sometimes receives the same Event Grid event twice and events don't always arrive in the order they were published. Is this expected?
o: Yes; delivery is at-least-once and unordered, so handlers must be idempotent
No; Event Grid guarantees exactly-once, ordered delivery to each handler
Only if dead-lettering is disabled; with a DLQ, delivery is exactly-once
Only for CloudEvents; the Event Grid schema keeps events in order
e: Retries can cause duplicate deliveries, and events are delivered independently, so ordering isn't guaranteed. Handlers should be idempotent, for example by tracking event ids, and use eventTime or sequence data if order matters. This is true for both schemas and regardless of dead-lettering.

q: You want to be notified when a secret in Key Vault is about to expire so a function can rotate it. Which Event Grid event should the function subscribe to, and when does it fire?
o: SecretNearExpiry, 30 days before the expiration date
SecretExpired, which fires 30 days before expiration
BlobCreated, which fires when the secret is rotated
VaultAccessPolicyChanged, which fires once a day
e: Key Vault publishes SecretNearExpiry when the current version of a secret is about to expire; the event fires 30 days before the expiration date. That gives time to create a new version. SecretExpired fires only once it has already expired, and the other events are unrelated.

q: A SaaS platform must publish events for thousands of tenants, each with its own subscribers, while managing authentication and partitioning centrally. Which Event Grid feature fits?
o: Event domains
A separate Azure subscription per tenant
One custom topic per event type with no tenant information
Service Bus sessions
e: Event domains manage large numbers of topics, typically one per tenant, under one endpoint, with centralized authentication and access control per domain topic. Separate subscriptions per tenant are unmanageable, a topic without tenant information can't isolate subscribers, and Service Bus sessions are a messaging feature.

q: Your Event Grid handler returns HTTP 400 Bad Request for a malformed event. What does Event Grid do?
o: It doesn't retry; the event is dead-lettered if configured, else dropped
It retries the event 30 times over 24 hours, like any other error
It sends the event on to all the other subscriptions on the topic
It disables the subscription until the handler is fixed and redeployed
e: Event Grid treats some errors, such as 400 Bad Request and 413 Request Entity Too Large, as failures that retrying won't fix, so it doesn't retry them and moves the event to dead-letter storage if configured. Transient errors like 503 are retried with backoff. Subscriptions aren't disabled by individual failures.

q: Using the Azure CLI, how do you create an event subscription on a custom topic that dead-letters to a blob container and stops retrying after 10 attempts or 2 hours?
o: az eventgrid event-subscription create ... --deadletter-endpoint <container-id> --max-delivery-attempts 10 --event-ttl 120
az eventgrid topic create ... --deadletter-endpoint <container-id> --max-delivery-attempts 10 --event-ttl 120
az servicebus queue create ... --max-delivery-count 10 --default-message-time-to-live PT2H --enable-dead-lettering-on-message-expiration
az storage container create ... --name deadletters --event-ttl 120 --max-delivery-attempts 10 --account-name <storage>
e: Dead-letter destination and retry policy are set on the event subscription: --deadletter-endpoint takes the storage container resource ID, and the retry policy uses max delivery attempts and event TTL in minutes. Topic creation doesn't define retries, and the Service Bus and Storage commands configure other services.

q: In the Event Grid event schema, which property identifies the publisher-defined path to the event subject, such as /blobServices/default/containers/images/blobs/cat.jpg?
o: subject
eventType
topic
dataVersion
e: subject is the publisher-defined path to the event subject, which is what subjectBeginsWith and subjectEndsWith filters match. eventType names the kind of event (for example Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated), topic is the full resource path of the event source, and dataVersion is the schema version of the data object.

q: A subscriber wants blob events delivered from a system topic, but only for one of the storage account's containers. Which filter does Microsoft show for limiting events to a specific resource path?
o: subjectBeginsWith set to the resource path prefix
includedEventTypes set to the container name
An advanced filter on topic with StringIn
isSubjectCaseSensitive set to true
e: The filtering guide uses subjectBeginsWith (or the --subject-begins-with CLI parameter) to limit events to a specific resource, because the subject contains the resource path. Event types describe what happened, not where, and case sensitivity only changes how subject filters compare text.

q: You create a webhook subscription in the portal. Where do you enable dead-lettering and customize the retry policy?
o: The event subscription's Additional features tab
The custom topic's Networking and identity blade
The storage account's lifecycle management policy
The Function app's host.json extension settings
e: In the portal, the event subscription's Additional features tab is where you enable dead-lettering to a blob container and customize the retry policy, while the Filters tab holds event type, subject, and advanced filters. Topic networking, storage lifecycle rules, and host.json don't configure Event Grid delivery.

q: An Azure Function uses the Event Grid trigger. What do you need to do about the subscription validation handshake?
o: Nothing; the trigger handles validation for you
Write code that echoes the validationCode back
Disable validation on the topic for functions
Use the CloudEvents schema so no handshake runs
e: When you subscribe with the Azure Functions Event Grid trigger, Event Grid authenticates with the function's key and the trigger extension handles validation, so no custom handshake code is needed. You only implement the handshake yourself for generic HTTP webhooks. Validation can't be disabled.

q: Which statement correctly describes Event Grid's retry behavior when an endpoint returns a transient error such as 503 Service Unavailable?
o: It retries with exponential backoff until the attempt limit or the TTL
It retries immediately every second until the endpoint recovers
It never retries 503 responses and drops the event right away
It uses a linear retry schedule that you choose on the subscription
e: For transient failures, Event Grid retries on an exponential backoff schedule, stopping when the maximum number of attempts or the event TTL is reached. The schedule isn't configurable, and 503 is a retryable status.

q: Your handler can process events far more efficiently in groups. Which delivery setting reduces the number of HTTP calls to a webhook?
o: Output batching: max events per batch and preferred batch size
A longer event time-to-live on the subscription's retry policy
Dead-lettering to a blob container that the handler reads in bulk
Advanced filters that group matching events into one request
e: Event Grid output batching delivers several events per HTTP request, controlled by max events per batch and preferred batch size on the event subscription. TTL, dead-lettering, and filters don't change how many events are sent per request.

q: A team plans to process a sustained stream of millions of IoT telemetry readings per second with replay and partitioned consumers. Which service fits better than Event Grid?
o: Azure Event Hubs
Azure Event Grid custom topics
Azure Key Vault
Azure App Configuration
e: Event Hubs is designed for high-throughput streaming of telemetry, with partitions, consumer groups, and retention for replay. Event Grid is designed for discrete, reactive events pushed to handlers, and Key Vault and App Configuration aren't messaging services.

q: You expect a temporary event subscription to be needed only until the end of a migration. How can you make Event Grid remove it automatically?
o: Set an expiration time on the event subscription
Set the event time-to-live to 1 minute on the topic
Set max delivery attempts to 1 on the subscription
Delete the topic when the migration has finished
e: An event subscription can have an expiration time, after which Event Grid removes it automatically. TTL and delivery attempts only control retries for individual events, and deleting the topic removes every subscription, not just the temporary one.

q: Event Grid can't deliver an event and dead-lettering isn't configured on the subscription. What happens to the event when retries are exhausted?
o: It is dropped
It stays in the topic forever
It is delivered to all other subscriptions
It is written to the Activity log for replay
e: Without a dead-letter location, Event Grid drops events once the retry policy (attempts or TTL) is exhausted. To keep them, configure a blob container as the dead-letter destination. Topics don't store events indefinitely, and the Activity log doesn't hold event payloads.
